device: Coral USB Edge TPU (USB 3.0, 5000M), host AMD Ryzen 7 8845H / 16 threads
what: EfficientDet-Lite1 full-scope pruning ladder, 19 rungs, exported so that EVERY operator maps to the Edge TPU (305/305, 0 on CPU). Three columns on ONE build, but not on one artifact: parameter reduction and int8 COCO val2017 mAP are measured on the quantized tflite (on CPU); on-device latency and the operator mapping are measured on the edgetpu_compiler output of that same tflite.

export.path: PyTorch -> litert-torch (float32 tflite) -> ai-edge-quantizer static_wi8_ai8 -> buffers inlined -> edgetpu_compiler 16.0
export.why_not_onnx2tf: onnx2tf lowers effdet's BiFPN fusion to a rank-5 CONCAT/SUM and timm's SAME-pool to PADV2; both are unmappable, so the TPU subgraph stopped at the backbone (83 of 479 ops). Patching the model and keeping onnx2tf does not work either: it then emits the 32 BiFPN depthwise convs as grouped CONV_2D v6, which edgetpu_compiler cannot parse.
model_side_patches: effdet FpnCombine: torch.stack(nodes,-1).sum(-1) -> sequential adds. weight_method is 'sum' for the lite configs, so this is arithmetically identical; it removes the rank-5 ops.
timm MaxPool2dSame: F.pad(-inf)+VALID pool -> ceil_mode=True with no padding. Bit-exact for 48->24, 24->12, 12->6, 6->3 (verified max|diff| = 0.0); it removes PADV2.
toolchain_workarounds: ai-edge-quantizer writes buffers with (offset,size) past the end of the flatbuffer; edgetpu_compiler 16.0's older parser reads them as garbage and maps only 3 of 345 ops. Re-serialize with buffers inline.

ai-edge-quantizer smooths every tensor's min/max across calibration batches (qsv_utils.moving_average_update, smoothing_factor=0.95), which cost 0.020 mAP. The live call site is algorithm_manager.get_update_qsv_func(); replacing it with a true min/max update recovers it (0.29321 -> 0.31345, matching onnx2tf per-channel's 0.31352). ALL of these ablation figures were measured on the lamp -10% rung (pruned10pct_lamp_full), COCO val2017, 5000 images -- not on the dense rung, whose int8_mAP is 0.31748. The fix was then applied to the whole ladder (23 rungs re-evaluated).

litert-torch's PT2E path is unusable here: OptimizeLayoutTransposesPass aborts on the q/dq graph ('Attempting to convert non-NHWC compatible node to NHWC'). Float export + ai-edge-quantizer is the working route.

protocol.latency: src/etpu/runtime/bench.py in the edgetpu_ros image, 15 warmup + 100 invokes, random input, two independent passes; the model has no in-graph NMS so latency is input-independent (verified on Coral's official artifact: 58.70 ms random vs 59.19 ms real image)
protocol.mAP: families/detection/effdet/eval.py eval, full COCO val2017 (5000 images), int8 tflite on CPU + anchor decode/NMS, score-thresh 0.001
protocol.fp32_mAP_source: outputs/pruning_logs/efficientdet_lite1_coco-train2017_<criterion>_<pct>pct_full.json (per-rung, pulled from the cluster; final_eval.mAP). These supersede results/detection/full_scope_grid.json, which is missing the lamp-90 row. Note a stale local coco-val2017 set of per-rung files exists with the same rung names -- match on coco-train2017.

findings.mapping: 305 of 305 operators on the Edge TPU, 0 on CPU, at every rung. Coral's own efficientdet_lite1_384_ptq is 315/7; its 7 CPU ops are the postprocess tail this export leaves to Python. Every rung compiles to a SINGLE Edge TPU subgraph, so the graph is not being carved up and handed back and forth across the USB boundary either.

latency_law.reading: Within this family off-chip bytes are 0 at every lite1 rung, so the repo's off-chip law has nothing to act on. What is left is a large fixed floor plus a term linear in MACs. The floor is the accelerator's I/O: 0.42 MiB in + 2.48 MiB out per inference, at a measured return rate of 86.8 MiB/s, which puts the 2.90 MiB at 33.4 ms against a fitted floor of 35.0 ms -- 96% of it. That rate comes from a deliberate control, because this ladder CANNOT establish it: all 19 rungs return exactly 2.48 MiB and accept exactly 0.42 MiB, so the variable has zero variance along the pruning axis. See results/detection/io_floor_control.json, which also corrects the earlier prose here (the extra conv is 1.53 ms of arithmetic, not ~0.1 ms, and the rate is 86.8 MiB/s, not ~81 MB/s). Pruning cannot touch any of it: the head emits 810 channels at every rung.

channel_alignment.what: Replacing MACs with MACs computed on channel counts rounded up to a tile width W improves the fit, with a clear peak at W=64 (the Edge TPU's systolic array width). NOTE the baseline: r2_by_width['1'] = 0.9367 is NOT latency_law.r2 = 0.9352. The padded series is a second, independently computed MAC count -- aiedge-lab/channel_align.py traces every Conv2d through the model and sums up(cout)*up(cin)*k*oh*ow (dense) or up(cout)*k*oh*ow (depthwise), whereas the mmacs column comes from the cluster logs. Compare 0.992 against this series' own W=1 value of 0.9367, not against 0.9352.
channel_alignment.natural_experiment: lamp-80% (877 MMACs) and magnitude-50% (1034 MMACs) differ by 18% in raw MACs but 1.7% in padded-64 MACs; measured 43.45 vs 43.62 ms (0.4% apart).
channel_alignment.reading: Raw MACs span 3.4x across the ladder (1954 -> 574) but padded-64 MACs span only 1.6x (4892 -> 3041), and latency spans 1.29x from the dense rung to the 90% rung (52.404 -> 40.773 ms). Latency is NOT monotone in MACs at the top of the ladder: lamp-10 measures 52.995 ms, above the dense rung. Below the array width pruning buys accuracy loss and no time: cutting a layer from 88 channels to 40 costs the same as cutting it to 64 -- but this layer-level equality is inferred from the whole-model fit, NOT tested at layer granularity. Channel census, counting the output channels of every Conv2d (213 of them): the unpruned rung has 6.6% below 64 channels and 95.3% at a multiple of 8; the deepest rung has 24.4% and 67.6%. An earlier version of this paragraph quoted 7% / 99% / 32% / 59%, which mixed three different counting bases -- see `supersedes` in results/detection/channel_census_lite1.json, which is now the source for all of this.

int8_cost_depends_on_criterion.what: int8 loss relative to the same rung's fp32 mAP grows with the pruning ratio, and the two criteria have different shapes: lamp is flat then knees, magnitude_l2 is linear from the start.
int8_cost_depends_on_criterion.reading: lamp holds the dense rung's int8 cost (about -1.4%) all the way out to the 60% rung and only then knees: -2.5% at 70%, -3.3% at 80%, -7.4% at 90%. magnitude_l2 is already -2.3% at the 10% rung and degrades roughly linearly to -7.7% at 90%. The magnitude/lamp ratio runs 1.05x to 3.48x with its worst point at the 30% rung (see magnitude_over_lamp_ratio); excluding the 90% rung, where both models are broken anyway, it is 1.61x to 3.48x. A linear fit describes magnitude_l2 well (R^2=0.92) but not lamp (R^2=0.54) -- read the per-rung numbers, not the slope. How far this is a reason to prefer lamp IN ITS OWN RIGHT is limited: on the RELATIVE column the criterion term is statistically absent once the rung's fp32 level is controlled for (R^2 0.9484 -> 0.9485 on adding a criterion dummy, t=+0.15, n=18). A real but small effect does survive on the ABSOLUTE drop: mean fp32-minus-int8 is 0.00511 for lamp against 0.00717 for magnitude_l2, a factor of 1.40 (dummy t=-3.70, n=18). State it that way. Untested mechanism: magnitude's global ranking narrows some layers far enough that the surviving weights' dynamic range widens.

findings.not_the_cause: The 0.020 mAP that separated this export from onnx2tf per-channel was NOT quantization granularity (both per-channel, verified by scale counts), NOT the algorithm key (OCTAV 0.29287 vs MIN_MAX 0.29321), NOT the BiFPN rewrite (keeping stack+sum gives 0.29363), and NOT input-tensor clipping (pinning the input range alone is worth +0.001). It was the smoothed activation calibration. Every figure in this paragraph is the lamp -10% rung (pruned10pct_lamp_full), COCO val2017, 5000 images.

open: efficientdet_lite2 WAS carried further after this file was written. Its ladder finished 2026-08-26 (19 fp32 rungs) and its int8 + Edge TPU artifacts were rebuilt 2026-08-27 (340/340 mapped); the int8 mAP and on-device latency columns were both measured 2026-08-28, so that ladder now carries the same four columns as this one. See results/detection/full_mapping_ladder_lite2.json, whose latency_law finding fits a 46.43 ms floor against this file's 34.95 ms and confirms io_floor_control.json's 86.8 MiB/s out of sample. lite2 is still excluded from every fit in THIS file, which is a lite1-only ladder.

WITHDRAWN. This entry used to read 'lite2 quantizes much worse than lite1: -5.9% at the dense rung against lite1's -1.4%'. That -5.9% was measured on the defective --pool-ceil lite2 export -- a network whose P7 level was 3x3 instead of 4x4 -- so it never described EfficientDet-Lite2. Re-measured on a correct build with the same harness, lite2's dense int8 loss is -1.65% against lite1's -1.38%: comparable, not 4x worse. results/detection/full_mapping_ladder_lite2.json carries the full column.

Full mapping is not the fastest configuration on a strong host: a partial map that leaves the 810-channel heads on the CPU measured 26.96 ms against 52.78 ms, because it returns 0.26 MiB instead of 2.48 MiB. Two caveats on those two numbers. 52.78 ms is the lamp -10% rung's median from the FIRST bench pass, taken before the calibration fix -- the dense rung of this ladder is 52.404 ms. And 26.96 ms has no committed measurement behind it; it survives as prose only. What full mapping buys is not latency on this host, it is that the detector stops competing for host CPU at all. Whether that trade is favourable is a property of the deployment host and its CPU load. Measuring it is deliberately OUT OF SCOPE for this repository, which measures the accelerator; it belongs with the downstream system's own benchmarks. Always report the host alongside a split.
